cranelift-entity: more efficient EntitySet implementation

#### Feature

The `EntitySet` type declared in `cranelift/entity/src/set.rs` is a fairly standard implementation of a bit-set. However, it uses 8-bit chunks in the `EntitySet::elems` storage vector. It should use a size closer to the width of a machine word.

#### Benefit

Using a larger size should give a small performance improvement.

#### Implementation

I'd prefer if `elems` were a `Vec<usize>`. Then the number of bits in each element is:

```rust
const BITS: usize = core::mem::size_of::<usize>() * 8
```

All the places which use the constant `8` should instead refer to `BITS`, and `7` should be replaced with `BITS - 1`.

If someone wants to tackle this, it would also be great if you could add doc-tests for the methods on this type while you're there. If you do, you may be able to remove the existing tests as they should be redundant with reasonably comprehensive doc-tests.

#### Alternatives

We can always leave this alone; it's not terrible as-is.

raw_text:
Yes this can be used instead of manually using EitherOf* and keeping track of which EitherOf*::A/B/C... was already used.

A simple usage example is in the PR (https://github.com/leptos-rs/leptos/pull/2900/files#diff-6edbb281543fc38e436f246c07e6d225c8fddfc49b6cf2e05dfbac26f9e5b5ddL140) 

```rust
    if let Some(node_ref) = node_ref {
        Either::Left(action_form.node_ref(node_ref))
    } else {
        Either::Right(action_form)
    }
```

```rust
    either!(node_ref,
        Some(node_ref) => action_form.node_ref(node_ref),
        None => action_form,
    )
```

Altough I have to admit in the normal `Either::Left/Right` case there is not much difference but when the `EitherOf*` gets to a higher number the macro is more readable.  
e.g. if have an enum with different variants or a nested Result/Option:

```rust
let result: Result<Option<i32>> = Ok(Some(1));
either!(result,
        Ok(Some(id)) => view! { <User id /> },
        Ok(None) => view! { <NotFound /> },
        Err(err) => view! { <ErrorScreen err /> },
)
```

which turns into

```rust
map result {
        Ok(Some(id)) => EitherOf3::A(view! { <User id /> }),
        Ok(None) => EitherOf3::B(view! { <NotFound /> }),
        Err(err) => EitherOf3::C(view! { <ErrorScreen err /> }),
)
```

Again not a big difference 😅 but now lets imagine you need to add another arm to the map. With the macro you simply add a new arm and are done, with the manual `EitherOf*` you need to replace all the `EitherOf3` with `EitherOf4`.


Overall I just think it's a nice improvement of the either_of crate.

Hi again, just wanted to let people here know that I've released a version 0.2 of [mdbook-i18n-helpers](https://github.com/google/mdbook-i18n-helpers/). This version changes how the text is extracted: paragraph are now unwrapped, headings are stripped of `#`, and tables are translated on a cell-by-cell basis.

A normalization tool is included to help you convert old translation files to the new format — we have [~18 translations](https://github.com/google/comprehensive-rust/tree/main/po) now for Comprehensive Rust, so it's important for us to have a migration path for those files.

I would be very interested in feedback if you try it out! Thanks :slightly_smiling_face:

Many of the failures are either warnings because the crates need pull request to remove deprecated options, or because rustfmt emits warnings or errors that the user cannot do anything about. 

If there is nothing that the user can do about a warning or internal error, then the diagnostic should IMO be opt-in (e.g. behind a `rustfmt --debug-output` or similar).

I've tried to enable these diagnostics here because even if they are opt-in, they should be fixed at some point. However a "red" allowed to fail travis build bot because of a warning can hide a change that actually breaks the build so... I did not know what the right way to proceed was here and did not wanted to add all buildbots twice...

Replacing native C types (Windows & Mac vs Linux)

Bindgen nicely replaces occurrences of native C types with Rust types. For example:
```C
#include <stdint.h>

typedef struct
{
    const uint8_t b[16];
} MunGuid;
```

results in:

```rust
#[repr(C)]
#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
pub struct Guid {
    pub b: [u8; 16usize],
}
```

It works. Lovely! One problem, once we run CI, it turns out that Ubuntu also generates this additional line

```rust
pub type __uint8_t = ::std::os::raw::c_uchar;
```

Even though bindgen is able to deduce that `uint8_t` is supposed to be `u8`, it still adds the `__uint8_t` type to the generated bindings.

One possible solution that I came up with to resolved this is to blacklist the `__uint8_t` type, but then bindgen stops automatically generating the `#[derive(Clone, Copy)]` attributes.

Is there a way to prevent the generation of "replaced" types?

raw_text:
Use `anyhow` for errors, so we can get backtraces

One thing that slows down Naga debugging is that errors are printed without a backtrace to indicate where they originated. Debugging means searching the tree for places where the given error might be raised, and then figuring out which site is responsible for the problem. This adds a few minutes to the debugging time that are totally unnecessary.

The `anyhow` crate has an `Error` type that could help us with this:

- It captures backtraces if the [right environment variables][backtrace] are set.
- It implements `From<E>` for any `E: std::error::Error + Send + Sync + 'static`, so you can just put it in a function's return type, and all the `?` operators will just do the conversion for you.
- The conversion is what captures the backtrace, so you get the location of the first `?` operator that touched the error.
- It supports downcasting to concrete error types, so you can still handle specific errors if you want.
- It's feasible to only use `anyhow::Error` in the rootward end of the call tree, there's no need to convert the entire source tree at once. You'll just get backtraces as localized as your use of `anyhow`.

The disadvantages are:

- The error types of the `Result` values in the tree become less specific.
- Capturing a backtrace is expensive compared to creating a bare error value, so code that generates and handles errors as a matter of course (the GLSL front end constant solver, for example) probably should not use `anyhow`.
- Another dependency, another layer of abstraction and mystery.

[backtrace]: https://docs.rs/anyhow/1.0.48/anyhow/struct.Error.html#method.backtrace

raw_text:
Sharing here for transparency the result of an experiment done with [OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io/) to push traces to Jaeger.

The resulting code can be found in this [commit](https://github.com/qdrant/qdrant/commit/e36fd9415c14c37fa1f88ae5b1ed81d71e27b11b).

It uses the following crates:

- [https://crates.io/crates/tracing](https://crates.io/crates/tracing)
- [https://crates.io/crates/tracing-opentelemetry](https://crates.io/crates/tracing-opentelemetry)
- [https://crates.io/crates/tracing-subscriber](https://crates.io/crates/tracing-subscriber)
- [https://crates.io/crates/opentelemetry](https://crates.io/crates/opentelemetry)
- [https://crates.io/crates/opentelemetry-jaeger](https://crates.io/crates/opentelemetry-jaeger)

With this setup I was query and analyze traces locally.

![jaeger-overview](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/606963/204790762-e9e83d1e-0f45-48ac-b22d-97569d346dec.png)

![consensus-thread](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/606963/204790944-8098d7e5-d238-428b-9b6e-8dffc790dc52.png)

This works really nicely but it has a couple drawbacks:

- not easy to setup due to the amount of moving pieces
- annotating manually the code to instrument is a bit cumbersome

raw_text:
This has the potential to create massive headaches for Linux distributions which package Rust crates (namely Fedora Linux and Debian, and possibly other, less popular distributions).

For example, the mapping between crate names and package names is currently unique in Fedora (crate `$CRATE` is packaged as `rust-$CRATE`), which works perfectly, since crates.io is a flat namespace. With this addition, this mapping will break - the colon (from the proposed namespace separator `::`) is not a valid character in RPM package names, and I'm pretty sure it's not a valid character in DEB either. There are only a limited number of valid punctuation characters that are usable in package names that are not already clashing with valid characters from crate names - only `.` and `+` currently come to mind ... so it will make implementing support for this feature possibly quite tricky for us.

A little more of a heads-up would have been nice ... 🙇🏻‍♂️

raw_text:
First of all, I like the idea of the PR and how it can make it much easier to get started with Tauri. I do have a few suggestions though:

First, I think that the CRA app files should be at the root level, with the `src-tauri` folder inside of it. It's how all the examples and the Vue CLI plugin are structured. The issue with Scala using `target` for dist isn't really a problem since Tauri dist is in `src-tauri/target` (although I do see how it could cause some confusion). Having a different structure than an existing CRA app with Tauri added via `tauri init` seems like unnecessary fragmentation. I think 95-99% of users will be using a JS framework and have a `package.json` anyway and sharing it would be easier to manage. Lots of new developers may try to install deps for their JS app into the tauri `package.json` and would be confused when it doesn't work.

Second, maybe we could automatically set [beforeDevCommand](https://tauri.studio/en/docs/api/config#build.beforeDevCommand) to start the CRA dev server so that `yarn tauri dev` just works, instead of making the user run multiple commands (same for build).

Third, I think there should be two separate commands for using a recipe and adding to an existing app (like @jbolda suggested). Maybe `tauri create` for creating a new app with a recipe, and `tauri integrate` (or `tauri init`) for adding to an existing app. I think this will make the process easier to understand for new developers trying to decide how to get started with Tauri.

Finally, I'm a little worried that this may be out of scope for the Tauri CLI. Creating a full list of recipes and keeping them updated isn't an easy task. We'd have to monitor for breaking changes in each CLI we use and then update Tauri CLI to support the latest version. What if a user wants to pass arguments to their framework CLI's init command? Do we have to create a passthrough for all the different config args for each framework? We also want to migrate the CLI to Rust at some point, and this would make that more difficult. A getting started doc page with instructions for each of the frameworks would be easier to maintain and give the user more control, although it would sacrifice some ease-of-use.

raw_text:
Have a briefly looked into this, the problem occurs when:
- `persist_egui_memory()` is false
- `NativeOptions.persist_window` is true
- zoom_factor is manually set by `ctx.set_zoom_factor()`, or `ctx.memory_mut(|m| m.options.zoom_factor = XXX)`, inside `AppCreator` or `eframe::App::update`

Far before zoom_factor is actually set by user codes, the initial window size is decided by:
https://github.com/emilk/egui/blob/cd3e9ea5b68107c34449f6355c7076ca5621bae4/crates/eframe/src/native/glow_integration.rs#L146-L161
Unfortunately, the initial window size is not that right since:
- Window size is calculated from `zoom_factor` and `inner_size_points`  persisted in storage
- `inner_size_points` is correctly loaded from STORAGE_WINDOW_KEY
- `zoom_factor` cannot be loaded from STORAGE_EGUI_MEMORY_KEY, since `persist_egui_memory()` is false. The default 1.0 is used
- the initial window size and default pos of area is based on these incorrect value, so finally the window shrinks and the area shifted

Ideas on resolving the problem:
1. persist `zoom_factor` under STORAGE_WINDOW_KEY instead of STORAGE_EGUI_MEMORY_KEY. A broken change though
2. provide an API like `ViewportBuilder.with_zoom_factor()` to allow user setting the value before App init_run_state

raw_text:
Both on Windows and Linux, the server thread seems to terminate properly. I've tested it by printing a line within the `spawn` closure.

`reuse_address(true)` could be the reason why it doesn't show an error when starting up for the second time and binding the same post and address again.
https://github.com/actix/actix-web/blob/6a0cd2dced8b085865e966e2d40baf1b8ad9d640/src/server.rs#L573

I'm not sure what the underlying issue is, but I've tried just `TcpListener::bind` and it "unbinds" just fine as the `TcpListener` gets out of scope on Windows. Perhaps it's something in https://github.com/rust-lang-nursery/net2-rs/blob/master/src/socket.rs as it's part of `net2-rs`. There would be some unsafe code there, but perhaps it's just missing a `Drop` implementation somewhere. Should I file a bug with `net2-rs`/do you think it might be coming from there?

It may be nice to just use `TcpListener`, if possible. But I'm not sure if it's as capable and if that's desireable. I just had a brief look so far and I saw that the `Socket` is converted to `TcpListener` in the end - if I got that right.

There might be something custom possible though that is still generic enough but has perhaps better semantics/ergonomic then boxing. But that's a whole different discussion... I think for now boxing works just fine with the downcasting... But that's just my POV. All I know is it needs a decision and if I learned anything from the internal rust language discussions that I lurk, it just needs to be a decision even if not perfect

Restarted from master of 5 June 2020, and now I am stuck in an attempt to change the return type of weight.scorer from Box < dyn Scorer > to Rc < RefCell < dyn Scorer>>.
I marked the commit twophase-20200607.

The problem for this is that the downcast:: < TermScorer> method is not available on dyn Scorer, even though Scorer extends downcast_rs::DownCast. 
Normally in such cases the compiler adds a suggestion to use a trait implementing the method, in this case I would expect that trait to be downcast_rs::DownCast. There is no such suggestion, and adding use downcast_rs::DownCast; results in an error message that the trait is not used.

Any idea on how to get this working?

When I disable all the code using the downcast to TermScorer, the tests pass, except for test_boolean_termonly_intersection, as expected, but I prefer to keep the TermScorer specialisations.
The disabling of the TermScorer downcast is on the twophase branch of today, two commits after twophase-20200607.

Add an accessor for the `Connect` implementation inside a Client to allow bypassing the connection pool.

I use hyper to (among other things) talk to Docker over TCP. Docker's API is primarily HTTP, however, the attach command hijacks the HTTP connection (see https://docs.docker.com/engine/api/v1.41/#operation/ContainerAttach).

I added this accessor to get the connection outside of the pool, and then use into_parts to break it into the raw i/o object to do the necessary communication.

raw_text:
I was looking through this repo to see whether anyone had translated from [emacs regexp syntax](https://www.gnu.org/software/emacs/manual/html_node/emacs/Regexps.html) using regex-syntax yet (my eventual goal is to produce an emacs native module). I'm pretty sure I could do that by transpiling the emacs regexp pattern string to a [`regex_syntax::ast::Ast`](https://docs.rs/regex-syntax/latest/regex_syntax/ast/index.html), since the AST looks pretty simple, and emacs regexps don't have any special features: it pushes that to the language instead.

As mentioned by @db48x in https://github.com/rust-lang/regex/issues/962#issuecomment-1446384219, emacs provides a high-level `rx` sexp notation, but I think that actually aligns with @BurntSushi's framing of "using your programming language features to assemble the regex" from https://github.com/rust-lang/regex/issues/962#issuecomment-1446263381! So I was hoping to demonstrate that regex-syntax makes that sort of thing possible *without* implementing that sort of higher-level abstraction itself directly (this is actually what makes it more generic/reusable)!

At first glance I think e.g. `emacs-regexp-syntax` can just be its own crate that depends on `regex-syntax` and generates a `regex_syntax::ast::Ast`, and I can propose upstreaming any extensions I need from the generic regex-syntax AST to this repo (although this seems unlikely to be necessary). I can then have another crate `emacs-regexp` which depends on `regex-automata` and exposes the emacs native module interface.

@BurntSushi is that how you would suggest architecting this if I wanted to interface other regexp interfaces to `regex-syntax` and co?

EDIT: started this in https://github.com/cosmicexplorer/emacs-regexp!

raw_text:
Markdown parsing in doc comments for help messages Tracking Issue

This tracks the feature `unstable-markdown` that implements compile time markdown parsing in the derive macros.

## Implemented Markdown features
| markdown | output | comment |
| - | - | - |
|  paragraph | joined on one line, surrounded by empty line |
| `# heading` | bold + underline + surrounded by empty line | default style for heading |
| `![image]()` | alt text | anyone feeling sixel?!|
| `<html>` | verbatim |
| `> blockquote` | ![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/3eec1b6e-fcc5-4293-9bb5-1fa1e869b270) | alternatively could use `>` |
| code block | ![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a3ce198c-a4e1-43d9-9a42-bd77dc2733c6)| same styling as `` `code` ``|
| (un)ordered lists | ![ordered list example](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/880b93b9-b19c-445e-9605-280f41dff941) | |
| `*emphasis*` | italic |
| `**strong**` | bold |
| `~stikethrough~` | strikethrough |
| `[link](url)` | underlined alt text + OSC 8 |
| `` `inline code ` `` | bold | default style for literal |
| ` --- ` hrule | `---` surrounded by empty lines |
| ` \| tables \| ` | verbatim |
| `\\\n` and `  \n` hard break | ends line |

## Open Questions
- [ ] unicode support i.e. `•` for bullet lists, `Options::ENABLE_SMART_PUNCTUATION` for `pulldown_cmark`, unicode lines for blockquotes
- [ ] using the default clap styling for code makes it the same to bold.
- [ ] should we make images a link to the image source
- [ ] should we add custom html tags a la https://docs.rs/color-print/latest/color_print/ this would allow users to use colors without us actually supporting runtime style information.
- [ ]  should we use other enumeration for nested lists? e.g. `a.`, `b.` and `i.`, `ii.`? we could use https://docs.rs/nominals for that
- [ ] styling for code blocks and block quotes
- [ ] separate control of OSC 8 for links & colors
- [ ] option to display URLs next to links.
- [ ] option to diplay URLs at the end of the help.

## Markdown Parser
See https://github.com/rosetta-rs/md-rosetta-rs for a comparison of parsers.

### `pulldown-cmark`
Same behavior as rustdoc (options for reference https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/59588250ad973ce69bd15879314c9769e65f36b3/compiler/rustc_resolve/src/rustdoc.rs#L244-L250).

But higher compile times, runtime performance probably not as impactful as we are doing it at compile time.

### `minimad`
Had some parsing issues but might be fixable.

Hi @ealmloff,

I've been working on the suggestions you provided, and I wanted to share my findings so far:

> (if I understood correctly)

1. For events, we're currently using `tao_waker`, which is initialized during the creation of `WebViewInstance`.
2. `WebViewInstance::new()` is called initially during app launch.
3. Later, when attempting to create a `new window`, `WebViewInstance` is being invoked again, but it gets stuck within the `window.build()` method.

You suggested queuing the `create new window` event, but I'm unclear on the exact location for this in the code. I tried using `send_event(NewWindow_event)`, but it seems that this only queues the event—it doesn’t actually create a new window. To open a window, we still need to create a `WebViewInstance`, which is where the process gets stuck.

Any further guidance on where  & how to queue this event would be greatly appreciated. Thanks for your help!

The problem with this code was discovered during debugging the deadlock. Reproduce scenario: write overlapping points into index-able collections until it stuck.

 Based on the stacktrace of the processes - this part of the code _should not_ be locked, but it is.
 The current assumption is that `try_write_for` doesn't work as we expected.
 
 Removing of `try_write_for` makes deadlock disappear, at least on the scenario we are trying.
 
 Initially, the `aloha_random_write` was not introduce to fix any problem, but more like a premature improvement to a hypothetical problem, which is actually was handled differently (by ordering locks of the segments), so I think that it is ok to remove it completely and leave with simplified version

Yes. I ran into the same problem. This was the [PR that added the check to `regex`](https://github.com/rust-lang/regex/pull/504), and this was the [PR that removed the dependency on `unreachable`](https://github.com/Amanieu/thread_local-rs/pull/13). Given that the `unreachable` and `void` crates are effectively micro-crates that are also, in practice, unmaintained, I would suggest lobbying the maintainers of `smallvec` to drop them as dependencies. It's probably a good idea to do that regardless of the minimal version check. cc @mbrubeck 

It looks like this was discussed in https://github.com/servo/rust-smallvec/issues/128, but we don't need to bump the MSRV to do this. They can just inline what they need from `unreachable` directly since there's so little code. In the process, they'll drop two dependencies from a very large number of crates in the ecosystem.

raw_text:
Hey, I'm not sure that the search-and-replace you suggested works with what I had in mind, But I agree that using wasm for preprocessing is a quite heavy requirement, and there has not really been any open issues which states that parsing and re-parsing is a bottleneck. I kind of noticed that there were few open issues asking for a plugin system, and some suggesting a wasm based plug-in system, which made me think of unifying all of them, but that might not necessarily be a good idea, as you have pointed out.

I feel that passing around a parsed structure would be a better choice, rather than passing raw markdown ;  as any (external) preprocessor that needs only raw markdown, can easily work as a find-and-replace thing as you suggested on raw files. Preprocessors would be specifically for conditionally/ programmatically transforming input, based on what is the input, for which I think 99% of time one will need parsed markdown. Even though it will tie mdBook to pulldown-cmark, I think it is a good parser, and unless you have any reason why mdBook _might_ move away from it, it would be safe to tie the preprocessors to it as well.

I haven't checked out mdBook-katex much, but from its readme, it seems to generate static pages, which fits with rest of mdBook ( I don't think there is much dynamic hydration of pages generated by mdBook by default, is there?). It also provides support to various math rendering options, and support for latex-style macros. I will try taking a more detailed look later for what limitations or advantages might be for swapping built-in mathjax with katex.

So the primary reason not to do this is that encoding/decoding takes place at runtime, and adding another encoding adds to the binary size even if you never use it. Since we've upgraded to `serde_qs`, the form-encoded option can handle most data structures. Leptos controls both the client and the server end of your server functions. Is there a reason you want to use JSON other than familiarity? Like I said, adding another encoding is not a zero-cost thing.

EDIT: I guess with some refactoring we might be able to reduce this cost actually, but it will take some work so I'm still curious to hear the reasoning.

Literal string flag `-F` doesn't escape ripgrep flags

#### What version of ripgrep are you using?
`13.0.0`

#### How did you install ripgrep?
`cargo install ripgrep`

#### What operating system are you using ripgrep on?
Ubuntu 22.04 under WSL.

#### Describe your bug.
The `--fixed-strings`/`-F` flag does not properly search for strings that are also ripgrep flags.

#### What are the steps to reproduce the behavior?
```
rg --fixed-strings "--version"
```
Similar behavior when searching for any other valid ripgrep flag.

#### What is the actual behavior?
```
ripgrep 13.0.0
-SIMD -AVX (compiled)
+SIMD +AVX (runtime)
```

#### What is the expected behavior?
ripgrep does a search for the literal string `--version`.

#### Current workaround
Use a regex with escape characters.
```
rg "\--version"
```

This could probably avoid the need for callbacks in e.g. https://github.com/rust-windowing/winit/pull/1759 and probably smooth out a lot of other cases where we need to react with a return value to an event, rather than just acting on it.

Not sure which option I prefer, but I think a decision needs to be made.

hyper::Uri does not seem to parse URIs that do not have a host field

The `Uri` parser does not appear to be able to handle URIs that do not provide a `host` field.

I realize that the `hyper::Uri` module might not be intended to provide a complete URI implementation, so maybe just a mention of this in the docs is good enough.

Anyway, here's the issue: Omitting a `host` field causes the parser to fail with `InvalidFormat`.

For example, RFC 8089 defines the `file` schema, allowing local files to omit host. Both `file:///` and `file:/` are allowed. RFC 3986 does not require a host field after a scheme. But this test fails on the `from_str()`.

```rust
    #[test]
    fn should_parse_file_scheme() {
        let uri = hyper::Uri::from_str("file:///foo/bar").expect("Should parse URI with no host");
        assert!(uri.host().is_none());
    }
```

Tested on Hyper 0.14.4

Allow escaping `#` when using the x flag

It's nothing really important, but it would be nice if one could escape a literal `#` so it doesn't start a comment when using the `x` flag.

The current workaround is using the ASCII literal `\x23`, but something like `\#` would be clearer.

Workaround example:

``` rust
let markdown_headline = regex!(r"(?x)
    ^
    (?P<level>[\x23]+)  # A bunch of hash symbols
    \s
    (?P<title>.+)       # Title
    $
");
```

raw_text:
Old lock file format is never written anymore

**Problem**

It seems to no longer be possible to get the old lock file format written anymore. Running nightly toolchains which touch the file seem to update it causing me to have to nuke it (since we support and test older toolchains too).

This mainly affects my wish to test minimal versions where `-Z minimal-versions` forces it to use a newer toolchain which then blocks out testing with the older toolchain (to ensure compatibility).

**Steps**
1. `cargo +1.32.0 update`
2. `cargo +nightly update -Z minimal-versions`
3. `echo "Cargo.lock no longer works with 1.32"`

**Possible Solution(s)**

Support a flag to write out the old lock file format. It used to be auto-detecting and not upgrade, but that changed at some point.

**Notes**

Output of `cargo version`:

```
cargo 1.48.0-nightly (875e01232 2020-09-08)
```

> Unnamed fields are anonymous ones: gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Unnamed-Fields.html

How would it make any sense that those members do not get initialized?

>  I still think paddings are not unnamed members mentioned in the standard.

Given that padding is explicitly called out as "unnamed", I disagree with that reading.

Notice that this interpretation is not just mine, I took it from https://wiki.sei.cmu.edu/confluence/display/c/EXP42-C.+Do+not+compare+padding+data which explicitly quotes the above parts of the standard when talking about padding.

> I believe paddings are never indeterminate in C, so your SROA example is sound even though the padding bytes are unspecified values.

I don't follow. Uninitialized variables are indeterminate. Why would their padding not be...?

The standard is generally extremely vague about all this indeterminate/unspecified/trap representation business. I think it is much clearer to follow the [approach proposed for LLVM](https://www.cs.utah.edu/~regehr/papers/undef-pldi17.pdf), where "indeterminate" becomes `poison` and there's a proper formal definition. Unintiailized memory is `poison`. The only way to explain my example above is to say that copying a struct resets all padding to `poison`.

@amrbashir Ueli works perfectly as I would expect the behaviour to work. 

It opens the popup on the active screen, with multiple monitors, where the mouse currently sits. 

The popup works when the app are in full screen mode. 

It also restores focus to the previous app when the pop up is closed. 

I couldn't find anything regarding Activation Policy in Ueli, so i think you are correct, maybe the activation policy is not needed to produce this kind of app? 

I believe the code for the window management can be found [here](https://github.com/oliverschwendener/ueli/blob/dev/src/main/main.ts#L207-L272) 

There is also some more config for the window [here](https://github.com/oliverschwendener/ueli/blob/dev/src/main/main.ts#L557) 

`mainWindow.setVisibleOnAllWorkspaces(true, { visibleOnFullScreen: true });`, which might be setting the `NSWindowCollectionBehaviorCanJoinAllSpaces` 

There is a bit of code in electron for this [here](https://github.com/electron/electron/blob/81c143318ba04c9aff2a5bcb80e4a1e3d55e019f/shell/browser/native_window_mac.mm#L343-L349) 

Interestingly, on windows, the app appears to minimise, where as on MacOS the window calls `show()` and `hide()`. I tried to dig into what these were doing when i originally looked into this with tauri but wasn't able to figure it out unfortunately.

Wanted: FreeBSD target maintainer

We have [lost our FreeBSD maintainer](https://github.com/rust-lang/miri/pull/2321#issuecomment-1205744150). Partial FreeBSD support exists in the codebase but it is not mentioned in the README as a supported platform. A lot of the test suite still fails, in particular everything that needs concurrency (due to https://github.com/rust-lang/miri/issues/3553).

Should we just leave it at that and see if another FreeBSD enthusiast shows up? I won't work on completing this support. But for now there is also little cost in just keeping it around; we can always remove it if/when it becomes a problem.

Should we just leave it at that and see if another FreeBSD enthusiast shows up? I won't work on completing this support. But for now there is also little cost in just keeping it around; we can always remove it if/when it becomes a problem.

Some API alignment (missing funcs) between `DataFrame`, `LazyFrame`, and `Series`

While implementing some larger-scale slice improvements for #3759, ended up also bringing a couple of `DataFrame`, `LazyFrame`, and `Series` methods into alignment (which helps make the common slice code "more" common ;)

These are standalone updates, so pushing them in advance of a slice-specific patch (likely later this weekend). One minor `slice` function improvement is included here for all three types, which is allowing the length param to be optional).

**DataFrame**
* Added `reverse`, to match `LazyFrame` (implementation remains `self.select(pli.col("*").reverse())`).

**LazyFrame**
* Expose `clone` method, to match existing methods in `DataFrame` and `Series`.

**Series**
* Added `reverse` in Rust and exposed up to Python, to match`LazyFrame` (and now `DataFrame`).
* Added `is_empty`, matching `LazyFrame` and `DataFrame`.

raw_text:
Merge imports

This PR adds a `merge_imports` config option, which merges multiple imports with the same prefix into a single nested import.

Thoughts:
1. We should not merge imports with different visibility or attributes.
2. In the previous review, @nrc [suggested to use different levels of merging over a simple boolean](https://github.com/rust-lang-nursery/rustfmt/pull/2475#issuecomment-367891258). I tried to use `usize` (0 means no merging, 1 means merging the top level segment, and so on), but it turned out to be kind of counter-intuitive IMO, so came back to true/false. 

Closes #1383. Closes #2452. Closes #2544.

raw_text:
I don't know what you mean by your assertion that they are "compatible."

There is literally an unbounded number of ways in which Python regexes are different than Rust regexes. And this generally applies to all pairs of regex engines unless they very strictly follow a standard. (Of which, generally speaking, only two are prevalent: POSIX and ECMA. Neither Python's regex engine nor Rust's regex engine follow either one.)

> I don't consider this issue invalid.

I want to be clear here that this issue is _definitively_ invalid within the scope of this project. That doesn't mean you don't have _a_ problem. You might have a problem on your end where you have a pile of regexes that worked with one regex engine and need to use them, unchanged, with some other regex engine. But that isn't really a problem I can help with and is in general not a problem that can be easily solved for any two regex engines. (Unless your patterns happen to incidentally behave the same, or as I mentioned above, the regex engines strictly adhere to an existing standard.)

> Do you have any particular guidance toward a solution for compatibility?

Well... of course not. Because I don't really know the structure of the problem you're trying to solve. All that's been presented to me here is a regex that works one way in Python and a seeming request to have it work the same way in Rust. But that will definitively not happen. As far as solving your problem in a different way, I don't know because I don't know what problem you're trying to solve. If, for example, these regexes are provided by end users and you've promised that the regex syntax is equivalent to whatever Python supports, then you need to use a regex engine with the goal of compatibility with Python's regex engine. (Of which, I believe only one exists. The `re` module in Python's standard library. The third party `regex` Python package on PyPI might also have enough compatibility to work for you.)

x64/newBE: improve lowering of CLIF `AtomicRmw` in the case where the old value is not required

PR #2149 provides an initial implementation of wasm atomics with x64/newBE.  That includes an initial lowering of CLIF `AtomicRmw` into a multi-instruction sequence that is general, but inefficient in the case where the old value at the location is not required, which is probably a common occurrence.  In such cases we could do much better by producing a single LOCK-prefixed integer read-modify-write instruction, for example `lock xorq $27, (amode)`.

If you want to write a blog with static site generation, you can use static segments like the official Dioxus blog does [here](https://github.com/DioxusLabs/docsite/blob/master/src/lib.rs#L88-L103). Or you can use the include-markdown crate to generate those routes for you. 

If you want the segment to be dynamic at runtime, you can use [incremental site generation](https://github.com/DioxusLabs/dioxus/blob/62719c309a26e5320b0bc9dde04a9d1689e351e4/packages/fullstack/src/launch.rs#L76) (combined with any of the [framework examples](https://github.com/DioxusLabs/dioxus/tree/62719c309a26e5320b0bc9dde04a9d1689e351e4/packages/fullstack/examples)) which renders static pages lazily when you first request the page and then caches the result.

If we did support completely dynamic segments in static site generation, it is unclear how we would determine what routes to generate static files for. The static site generator currently runs the SSR renderer for a set number of static routes, if the routes are dynamic, there could be a huge number of routes that are possible `/:route` could be anything from `/12342` to `/this_is_a_test`.

Yeah theres definitely a lot of work to do on the performance front. I think Transform gpu buffer construction also plays a role in this.

Off the top of my head, the clear improvements to be made are:

2. Implement instancing: #89 
3. Implement batching
4. Cut down on redundant work using the new Changed<T> api: #63 
5. Optimize hash functions used: #157
6. Reduce the amount of hashing in general
7. Cull objects not visible by the camera (as you're doing in your example above)

I think it makes sense to scope this issue to (1).

Seems ilke [this issue](https://github.com/DioxusLabs/dioxus/issues/2619#issuecomment-2220996050) provides some information on how to do this, so you could use onmounted event to get the web-sys HtmlDialogElement:

```
onmounted: move |e| { e.as_web_event().dyn_into::<HtmlDialogElement>().unwrap().show_modal() },
```

If you need to use it somewhere else, assign the HtmlDialogElement into a signal to use it.

Reuse rustls::ClientConfig across clients whenever possible

I have different incompatible client configurations per request which necessitates that I create a new client for every request. The client seems to internally create a new rustls::ClientConfig each time. This is expensive and seems to be killing performance.

Maybe allow the user to provide a ClientConfig, which the user can cache. This would override some client settings that modify the ClientConfig. By default the client could also use static ClientConfig instances for common configurations such as umodified keystore, TLS trust on / off, hostname vertification on / off.
